title: Netflix Takes on YouTube by Licensing Digital Publisher Videos Starting August

body:
Netflix is making its boldest move yet to capture the kind of casual, always-on viewing that YouTube has dominated for over a decade. Starting August 3, the streaming giant will begin licensing videos from popular digital publishers — bringing home tours, recipe clips, celebrity interviews, and short-form content directly to its platform.

What's Coming

Netflix has partnered with BuzzFeed Studios, Condé Nast titles including Vogue and Vanity Fair, Hearst Magazines brands like Elle and Cosmopolitan, and Penske Media outlets such as Variety and Rolling Stone. The licensed content ranges from three-minute clips to episodes past twenty minutes.

None of these videos are produced by Netflix. The company is licensing existing series that already have loyal audiences on YouTube — Architectural Digest's home tours, Bon Appétit's cooking videos, and Vanity Fair's celebrity lie detector tests.

The Strategic Play

Netflix has been expanding beyond traditional TV shows and movies, adding live sporting events, games, podcasts, and vertical clips. Publisher videos fit this trajectory. The timing follows a Bloomberg report that Netflix's biggest hits are losing half their audience by season two.

Can Netflix Compete With YouTube?

YouTube's advantage is that everything is free and powered by recommendations that keep users browsing. According to Nielsen, Americans spend roughly 12.9% of TV viewing time on YouTube — more than Netflix and Disney+ combined. Netflix remains paywalled and built for premium entertainment, not casual browsing.

But Netflix is betting it can answer a universal problem: what do you watch when nothing you want is on? Publisher videos represent low-cost content that fills dead time and keeps subscribers from opening YouTube.
